title: Speed and motion
ks3: Motion and forces: speed, distance-time graphs and relative motion
intro: How fast? Practise speed = distance ÷ time, units like m/s and km/h, reading distance-time graphs, and relative motion.
description: Free KS3 Physics speed questions with answers: speed, distance and time calculations, units, distance-time graphs and relative motion. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: Which is the formula for speed?
questions.hint: Speed tells you how far something goes in each second (or each hour).
questions.explain: Speed is the distance travelled in each unit of time, so speed = distance ÷ time.

questions.q: A car travels 100 m in 20 s. What is its speed?
questions.hint: Speed = distance ÷ time.
questions.explain: Speed = 100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 m/s.

questions.q: A cyclist rides 30 km in 2 hours. What is the average speed?
questions.hint: Divide the distance by the time.
questions.explain: 30 km ÷ 2 h = 15 km/h.

questions.q: A car travels at 20 m/s for 15 s. How far does it go?
questions.hint: Distance = speed × time.
questions.explain: Distance = 20 m/s × 15 s = 300 m.

questions.q: A runner runs 400 m at a steady 8 m/s. How long does it take?
questions.hint: Time = distance ÷ speed.
questions.explain: Time = 400 m ÷ 8 m/s = 50 s.

questions.q: A train travels 150 km in 1 hour 30 minutes. What is its average speed?
questions.hint: Write the time in hours first: 30 minutes is half an hour.
questions.explain: 1 hour 30 minutes = 1.5 hours. Speed = 150 km ÷ 1.5 h = 100 km/h.

questions.q: Sam runs 90 m in 15 s. What is Sam's speed?
questions.hint: Speed = distance ÷ time.
questions.explain: Speed = 90 m ÷ 15 s = 6 m/s.

questions.q: Mia skates 100 m in 20 s. Leo skates the same 100 m in 25 s. Who is faster?
questions.hint: They go the same distance. Who takes less time?
questions.explain: Over the same distance, the one who takes less time is faster. Mia: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s. Leo: 100 ÷ 25 = 4 m/s. Mia is faster.

questions.q: A swimmer swims 4 lengths of a 25 m pool in 80 s. What is the swimmer's average speed?
questions.hint: Work out the total distance first.
questions.explain: Distance = 4 × 25 m = 100 m. Average speed = 100 m ÷ 80 s = 1.25 m/s.

questions.q: A bus has an average speed of 30 km/h for a journey. What does this tell you?
options: On average it went 30 km in each hour, but its speed changed along the way
It went at exactly 30 km/h the whole time
It never went faster than 30 km/h
questions.hint: Buses speed up, slow down and stop at bus stops.
questions.explain: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. The bus went faster at some times and slower (or stopped) at others; 30 km/h is the steady speed that would cover the same distance in the same time.

questions.q: A family drives 120 km at an average speed of 80 km/h. How many hours does the journey take?
questions.hint: Time = distance ÷ speed.
questions.explain: Time = 120 km ÷ 80 km/h = 1.5 hours, which is 1 hour 30 minutes.

questions.q: Which of these is a unit of speed?
questions.hint: Speed is a distance divided by a time.
questions.explain: m/s means metres per second: a distance divided by a time. m is a distance, s is a time and N is a force.

questions.q: How many metres are there in 3.5 km?
A sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s. What is their speed in km/h?
questions.hint: Work out the speed in m/s first. Then: how many metres in an hour (3600 s)? How many km is that?
questions.explain: Speed = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 m/s. In one hour (3600 s) that is 10 × 3600 = 36,000 m = 36 km. So the speed is 36 km/h.

questions.q: A snail crawls at 0.5 cm/s. How many minutes does it take to crawl 1.2 m?
questions.hint: Change 1.2 m into centimetres first.
questions.explain: 1.2 m = 120 cm. Time = 120 ÷ 0.5 = 240 s, and 240 s = 4 minutes.

questions.q: What does the speed unit **km/h** mean?
questions.hint: The / means "per" or "in each".
questions.explain: km/h means kilometres per hour: how many kilometres are travelled in each hour. m/s means metres per second.

questions.q: A car travels at 72 km/h. What is its speed in m/s?
questions.hint: Change the kilometres into metres and the hour into seconds.

questions.q: The graph shows a cyclist's journey. What is the cyclist doing between 10 s and 20 s?
questions.hint: Does the distance change between 10 s and 20 s?
questions.explain: The line is flat: the distance stays at 50 m, so the cyclist is not moving.

questions.q: Use the graph. What is the cyclist's speed in the first 10 s?
questions.hint: Read the distance at 10 s, then divide by the time.
questions.explain: In the first 10 s the cyclist goes 50 m. Speed = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 m/s.

questions.q: Use the graph. What is the cyclist's speed between 20 s and 30 s?
questions.hint: Find how far the cyclist goes in those 10 s: subtract the two distances.
questions.explain: The distance goes from 50 m to 120 m, so 70 m in 10 s. Speed = 70 ÷ 10 = 7 m/s.

questions.q: Use the graph. What is the cyclist's average speed for the whole 30 s?
questions.hint: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, including the stop.
questions.explain: Total distance 120 m, total time 30 s. Average speed = 120 ÷ 30 = 4 m/s.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, what does a steeper straight line show?
questions.hint: A steeper line means more distance in the same time.
questions.explain: The steeper the line, the more distance is covered each second, so the speed is faster.

questions.q: The graph shows a skateboarder's journey. For how many seconds was the skateboarder stopped?
questions.hint: Look for the part of the line that is flat.
questions.explain: The line is flat from 10 s to 20 s: the distance stays at 40 m. So the skateboarder was stopped for 20 − 10 = 10 s.

questions.q: Use the graph. What is the skateboarder's speed between 20 s and 30 s?
questions.hint: How far does the skateboarder go in those 10 seconds?
questions.explain: The distance goes from 40 m to 100 m, so 60 m in 10 s. Speed = 60 ÷ 10 = 6 m/s.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, the line slopes **down** towards the time axis. What does this show?
options: The object is moving back towards where it started
questions.hint: The graph shows distance from the start. What is happening to that distance?
questions.explain: The distance from the start is getting smaller, so the object is coming back towards the start. A straight line sloping down means it comes back at a steady speed.

questions.q: Two cars drive the same way along a motorway. One goes at 30 m/s and the other at 25 m/s. How fast does the faster car pull away from the slower one?
questions.hint: Same direction: find the difference.
questions.explain: Moving the same way, the gap grows by 30 − 25 = 5 m every second: 5 m/s.

questions.q: Two trains travel towards each other on side-by-side tracks, at 40 m/s and 35 m/s. How fast does the gap between them close?
questions.hint: Opposite directions: both trains make the gap smaller.
questions.explain: Each second the gap shrinks by 40 + 35 = 75 m, so it closes at 75 m/s.

questions.q: A train moves forwards at 20 m/s. You walk towards the back of the train at 1 m/s. What is your speed compared with the ground?
questions.hint: The train carries you forwards, but you are walking the other way.
questions.explain: Compared with the ground you move 20 − 1 = 19 m/s forwards. Compared with the train you move 1 m/s backwards.

questions.q: You skate at 3 m/s. Your friend skates right beside you, the same way, also at 3 m/s. How fast does your friend seem to move compared with you?
options: 0 m/s, they seem to stay still
questions.hint: Does the gap between you change?
questions.explain: You both go the same way at the same speed, so the gap does not change: 3 − 3 = 0 m/s. Compared with you, your friend seems to stay still.

questions.q: A jogger runs along a path at 3 m/s. A cyclist 100 m behind rides the same way at 8 m/s. How many seconds does the cyclist take to catch up with the jogger?
questions.hint: First find how fast the gap closes. Both move the same way.
questions.explain: The gap closes at 8 − 3 = 5 m/s. Time = 100 m ÷ 5 m/s = 20 s.
